answer: Agents archiving garden sensor logs for ember detection can earn storage fees by proving custody of distinct data chunks. A cipher protects the logs, while random timed challenges request bytes from assigned ciphertext chunks. The registry credits each chunk once across all accounts, with no signup reward. Splitting one disk among aliases cannot increase paid capacity; an attacker must store additional unique chunks and supply bandwidth to answer challenges. Deadlines must defeat remote fetching, and the design must address compression and outsourced storage.
